Why Conservatives Should Root for Taylor Swift

Joshua L. Sohn

Taylor Swift is married—perhaps you’ve heard? She’s always been a mirror for others to project their hopes and visions, and her latest era is no different. As a country music ingenue in her early years, she was sometimes assumed to be conservative. As a New York-based pop star in the mid-2010’s, she was lionized as a paragon of girlboss liberalism. And consider her current incarnation—newly-married to a middle-America football star, singing out against cancel culture, socializing with Republican NFL wives and liberal musicians in equal measure. Call it her centrist or big-tent pivot: she’s never been more dominant across the cultural spectrum.

Pro-family thinkers should take note. As Swift continues to be the alpha-dog of American pop culture, she could have positive effects on family-related issues like romance, marriage, and kids.

Highlights

As Taylor Swift moves into her marriage-and-kids era, she could be a positive example of the benefits and pleasures of family life.
Post This

Contrary to the culture-war stereotype, liberal Americans are quite open to messages of monogamy, marriage, and children.
Post This

A Swift Rebound on Family Issues?

First, consider romance and a revival of dating for marriage. If Swift enters the Hollywood screenwriting business as rumored, she could help Hollywood break free from its long-standing aversion to romance. I don’t know precisely what a Swift-written feature film would look like, but it’s safe to say it would have some serious boy-meets-girl energy. And if you take the view that Hollywood’s retreat from romance is at least part of what’s fueling real-life Americans’ retreat from sex and dating, then Swift might help reverse that trend.

Next, consider marriage. Swift’s wedding was a major cultural event, and it may become even bigger when the veil of secrecy is lifted and more details become public. But her pro-marriage vibes go far beyond her wedding day. Just last month she was caught on national TV yelling “that’s my husband!” and pointing to her wedding ring after Travis Kelce scored a touchdown. It’s hard to imagine better PR for the institution of marriage.

Finally, consider kids. As Tim Carney has written, suppose Swift has kids soon and starts penning tender maternal ballads about them. Could that help counteract the common cultural message that motherhood is a brutal game not worth playing? It may have a better chance of success than anything else on the cultural horizon. Notably, the Institute for Family Studies’ 2026 report on American birth projections name-dropped Swift when stating that “celebrity fertility really is associated with the fertility of fans.” The paper went on to suggest that the demographic effect of Swift having kids could be larger than the effect of nationwide child tax credits.

There’s a lesson here: contrary to the culture-war stereotype, liberal Americans are receptive to messages of monogamy, marriage, children, community, and even religion.

If this all sounds like a social conservative’s wish list, that’s because it is. And it doesn’t stop there. For generations, social conservatives have criticized pop culture for celebrating libertinism, hedonism, and outre counter-culturalism. But Swift is about as outre as the apple pie (or bread) that she might be baking right now. In the weeks before her wedding, she made the gossip pages for such wild stunts as going out to dinner with her parents and writing a song for the new Toy Story movie.

For all these reasons, pro-family conservatives should be rooting for Swift. At minimum, they should end their weird hostility to her. Yes, Swift has endorsed Democrats, and she almost certainly is a Democrat herself. So much the better: in an age where Democrats are increasingly disinclined to marry and have kids, it’s helpful that the biggest Democratic celebrity is newly married and seems to be pursuing parenthood, too.

Babylon

For a distillation of these hopes and possibilities, consider one of Swift’s most recent and remarkable songs. On September 25, 2026, she released a quartet of new music, the best-received of which was the elegiac ballad “Babylon.” Part of the song is an ode to community and religion, referencing close-knit relatives with their “church dress on.” Another part is an apparent endorsement of monogamy over hookup culture, as Swift gently chides the unnamed subject of the song for playing the field instead of settling down with the one woman who truly loves him. And the denouement comes when Swift fast-forwards the subject’s life and sings about “all the best parts/And they’re all at home/She’s hanging Christmas lights with your son.” In the end, the subject of the song is revealed to be “[a] liberated libertine who then longed for home.”

Even more remarkable than the lyrics was the song’s reception in the mainstream media, such as The Cut. It was also praised in Elle as a song that

reveal[s] the cost of choosing status over love . . . it tells the story of a social-climbing man who grapples with what he left behind—his small town, good partner, and family—as he pursued wealth and a more materialistic life.

There’s a lesson here: contrary to the culture-war stereotype, liberal Americans are receptive to messages of monogamy, marriage, children, community, even religion. I should know—I live among liberal families who live lives that almost seem ripped from a Norman Rockwell painting.

Thus, while marriage and childbearing rates are declining among liberals in particular, cultural nudges could make a difference. There’s an openness to the messages that pro-family advocates want to send—as long as they come from the right messenger. I’d argue that Swift could be one of the best messengers, as a celebrity and brilliant communicator who has broad cultural cachet.

A Marriage and Kids Era

It goes without saying that Swift is entitled to live her own life; she has no obligation to serve as a role model. But she is a role model, nonetheless. And as she moves into her marriage-and-kids era, she could be a positive one when it comes to the benefits and pleasures of family life.

Joshua L. Sohn is an attorney and author in Washington, D.C. His writings have appeared at Family Studies, Public Discourse, America (the Jesuit Review), Commonplace, Plough, the Washington Examiner, and in numerous law reviews.
